thread.title: Facebook: 'Fundamentally Altered DNA' Means Profit Pressure - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)

author: Dan Victor, CFA
title: Facebook: 'Fundamentally Altered DNA' Means Profit Pressure - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)
text:
It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price, than a fair company at a wonderful price. - Warren Buffett
Facebook, Inc. (NASDAQ: FB ) is a fair company at a fair price, and that's not what investors should be looking for. I'm well aware of the bullish case involving the current "historically cheap" valuation multiples and forecast revenue growth story but just not impressed. I'm bearish on the stock because the negative headlines keep coming, and it's fundamentally changing the way investors think about the stock which translates into structurally lower multiples. In my opinion, the days of Facebook trading at +20x earnings are over. There's been enough damage to Facebook's corporate image that it no longer commands the same quality and growth premium.
Facebook, Inc. Monthly Stock Price Chart. Source - finviz.com
Shares are down 35% from its all-time high and without being dramatic; it's possible the stock never fully recovers. This article will explore why Facebook equity investors should not expect significant upside from the current level.
Altered DNA 2018 will be remembered as the year the company lost its air of invincibility. Facebook may have been "wonderful" during its epic climb from a $20 stock in 2013 to $220 last summer, but what's emerging out of the data breach scandals ( Cambridge Analytica among others ), U.S. congressional hearings, lawsuits, and changing regulation worldwide indicates the company is going to look different going forward.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg admitted as much when he made an end of the year type post on the network describing how 2018 was a challenging year. The key quote that was reported by the Seeking Alpha news team related to how Facebook has changed.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg Facebook Post Screenshot. Source - Facebook.com
We're a very different company today than we were in 2016, or even a year ago. We've fundamentally altered our DNA to focus more on preventing harm in all our services, and we've systematically shifted a large portion of our company to work on preventing harm. We now have more than 30,000 people working on safety and invest billions of dollars in security yearly.
The quote eloquently describes how the company is going to be spending a lot more money on things it previously didn't even consider as necessary. Facetiously, Mr. Zuckerberg is saying that the company has shifted its focus from simply growing and making money to public-relations damage control. In the short run, these changes are not positive for investors, and the long-term consequences remain uncertain.
FB EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
While the statement in December was newsworthy, the message was already known to the market and reflected in lower profit forecasts. To understand how significant the impact of this "altered DNA" has been on earnings, just look at current market consensus for EPS. Since late summer, prior to the Q2 earnings release, consensus EPS has trended lower.
Among 35 street analysts tracked by YCharts, EPS estimates since July are:
down 4% for 2018, revised lower from $7.79 to $7.50 down 18% for 2019, revised lower $9.27 to $7.62 down 20% for 2020, revised from $10.84 to $8.70 The 2020 EPS estimate of $8.70 per share is down from a previous estimate of $10.84 per share and back to the same level that was the consensus forecast in January of 2017 when coincidentally the stock price was around $135. Marking down an earnings forecast ~20% for each of the next two years is one way to explain the plunge in Facebook shares. Management has guided for operating expenses to grow 50-60% for the full fiscal 2018 and again 40-50%. A large part of this increase is in direct response to address the scandals and an attempt to minimize regulatory and litigation risks going forward. The result of higher expenses is simply operating margin pressure and lower profit growth.
FB Revenue (Quarterly) data by YCharts
The concern here for investors is that revenue growth will trail, and it's already slowing. Revenue estimates for the next two years are decelerating while consensus EPS growth for 2019 is an anemic 1.6%.

To be clear, a +20% revenue growth forecast for the next two years and average EPS of growth ~8% are numbers most companies would and should be envious, but for Facebook, it's sobering. When you take a deeper dive at how the company is changing, I believe there is downside to these estimates, and street price targets may still be cut. FB currently trades at ~18.0x next year earnings, and there's little to suggest this should or needs to be significantly higher.
FB PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts
Even if you think 18x is too low for Facebook's growth, a higher earnings multiple of something like 20x represents just 10% upside for the stock and, in my opinion, doesn't justify the higher risk here. Comparing earnings multiples to the largest six mega-cap tech stocks by market value; Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet, Inc. ( GOOGL ) ( GOOG ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Intel ( INTC ), I don't see any evidence to suggest Facebook should be trading at a premium to the group considering its unique challenges beyond broader macro trends. Microsoft and Alphabet each with a forward P/E ~22.75x are not facing the same type of imminent margin pressure and in their cases, an argument can be made that the business outlook improved in 2018. Facebook operating margin to end Q3 was reported at 42.11%, considering still surging expenses, this number will likely drop below 40% in 2019 and could be headed to the mid-30s, the lowest since 2015.
FB Operating Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts
The company now has over 33,606 employees, double the level from 2016, and this type of rapid growth typically creates managerial problems over cost controls. All things point to Facebook having a difficulty maintaining a high level of profitability.
FB Total Employees (Annual) data by YCharts
Multiples Contraction Playing around with implied forward price-to-earnings ratios helps to frame potential trading ranges and establish downside risk. Investment cases are made stronger when there is context behind the numbers. The modest 4% revision lower to 2018 forecast EPS last year on its own was not necessarily a disaster, but the story around it has been a bigger deal. The cumulative impact of the data scandals, slowing growth, weak guidance, questions regarding corporate governance, and overall poor sentiment will continue to pressure the stock.
FB data by YCharts
The biggest risk for investors is an earnings miss over the next year resulting in further revisions lower to growth forecasts. Facebook is currently riding an incredible 2-consecutive-quarter streak of "beating" EPS estimates. The company reports fiscal 2018 Q4 January 30th, and this apparent record will be on the line.
Facebook, Inc. Earnings Summary. Source Seeking Alpha /author compilation
An earnings miss possibly related to higher-than-expected operating expenses and lower margins would be detrimental to stock price performance. Should the company miss, expect further earnings revisions lower. A potential 5% revision lower to 2019 EPS estimates to $7.24 may be matched by further multiple contraction, and FB could trade at 16.0x forward earnings, representing a ~$116.00 share price and 15% downside from current level. On the other hand, a strong Q4 earnings report, coupled by firming guidance, could see an earnings multiple expansion to 20x driven by improved sentiment. Given the narrative around Facebook, I would err on the side of caution.
Conclusion
Facebook, Inc. P/E valuation matrix. Source: Author estimates
The matrix above demonstrates implied share prices for Facebook at varying levels of forward 2019 earnings multiples. I see the stock as presenting an unattractive risk-reward setup with upside generously set around ~$155 per share as a bullish case, and down to ~$115 as a bearish outcome this year. My recommendation is to avoid the stock. Investors on the sidelines that like the long-term growth story may be able to pick up shares lower with patience.
